newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Albright to put spotlight on Bosnia war crimes tribunal.
newsitem.headline: Albright to put spotlight on Bosnia war crimes tribunal.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright will focus on the prosecution of Bosnian war criminals on Wednesday, a troubled process that is viewed by experts as a major threat to the 1995 Dayton peace agreement.

In the Hague for a U.S.-European Union summit, she planned a side visit to the international war crimes tribunal to meet chief prosecutor Louise Arbour, who has repeatedly criticised the failure to arrest senior Bosnia faction leaders indicted for war crimes and bring them to trial.

A senior official who last week outlined details of a new U.S. campaign to re-invigorate the flagging Bosnia peace process said "bringing war criminals to justice" is now the administration's top priority.

But Washington has failed to make public any new plans to achieve that goal, a feature of the 1995 U.S.- brokered Dayton accords that experts say is essential to any hope of a lasting peace in Bosnia.

Albright last week publicly exhorted Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and Bosnian Serbs to turn over indicted war criminals in their jurisdictions. She and other officials warned that Washington would more vigorously use financial and other pressure to ensure all aspects of the Dayton accord are carried out.
Ambassador Robert Gelbard, the new U.S. Bosnia coordinator, failed Monday in the latest attempt to persuade Milosevic to comply with the Dayton peace accord and deliver indicted suspects to justice.

Albright is to meet Milosevic in Belgrade on Saturday in a further effort to press the Serbian leader on this and other issues. She attends NATO and Bosnia-related meetings in Sintra, Portugal on Thursday and Friday, then flies to Zagreb Friday. She visits Sarajevo and Brcko in Bosnia on Sunday.
Diplomats have predicted Milosevic would refuse to hand over war crimes suspects before Serbian elections due by the end of the year.
Belgrade refuses to deliver three senior Yugoslav army officers indicted in connection with atrocities in the Croatian town of Vukovar during the six-month Croatian-Serb war in 1991.

Four years since it was set up by the U.N. Security Council, the Hague tribunal has indicted 75 suspected war criminals, including former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and his army commander General Ratko Mladic, who remain at large like the majority of other suspects.

Only nine have been arrested and sent to The Hague, including Bosnian Croat prison camp commander Zlatko Aleksovski. Croatia handed him over last month only after U.S. threats to block major loans to the country.

Washington says it does not know the whereabouts of all the indicted suspects. But a senior U.S. official insisted "we're looking at every possible way to bring war criminals to justice" including a proposal for a special military unit to track down suspects for delivery to the Hague.

The NATO-led stabilisation force in Bosnia, which U.S. troops dominate, is not charged with ferreting out war criminals, although political leaders have insisted the troops would arrest suspects if they encoutered them in the normal course of business.
But so far they have not done so, fuelling suspicions that the Pentagon, which has resisted involvement with the war criminals issue, had a deliberate policy of avoiding suspects.

To get around this problem, U.S. officials have explored the creation a special military unit to track down indicted suspects. There has been some opposition from Europe but U.S. officials say this is not universal and the idea remains alive.

Theodor Meron, who helped the tribunal prosecute Bosnian Serb Dusan Tadic for war crimes in 1995, wrote in a recent article in Foreign Affairs magazine that "the international community has given the tribunal strong rhetorical support but little aid in enforcement."

He calls this a "disgrace" and says suspects could have been captured by the NATO-led forces "without serious casualties, especially with the help from the intelligence community. The risk was worth taking."
He asserted that the Dayton peace accords granted the NATO- led force sufficient powers to act but its leadership, "spearheaded by the United States, chose to hide behind a transparent fiction."

Meron noted the tribunal judges will complete their four- year terms in the fall and that there are suggestions that the United Nations should terminate the tribunal's mandate for Bosnia if more aggressive action is not taken.
